title: Al-Mani', the Preventer
tomorrow: Dadi's knee aches in the damp. what does she say to the ache?

lines: BAD LUCK, OR HARM HELD BACK?
TWO READINGS OF A CLOSED DOOR.
cards: The canceled flight. The party you weren't invited to that turned out to be a mess. The job that went to someone else.
Yesterday's question: rain wipes out round two of the paint day. Bad luck, or harm held back? The tradition keeps two honest readings of a closed door, and they don't cancel each other out.

teach.h: ONE READING: THE DOOR IS PROTECTION.
teach.b: Today's Name is Al-Mani', the Preventer, who withholds harm. The first reading says: the closed door is protection.

teach.h: YE HATE A THING WHICH IS GOOD FOR YOU.
teach.b: The Qur'an, in Pickthall's words: "it may happen that ye hate a thing which is good for you, and it may happen that ye love a thing which is bad for you. Allah knoweth, ye know not."
The Sufi teacher Ibn 'Ata'illah turned it into a riddle: sometimes He gives you by withholding, and withholds from you by giving. On this view, the rain on the paint day might be the gift.

teach.h: THE OTHER: THE DOOR IS A MIRROR.
teach.b: The second reading says: a closed door can also be a mirror.
The Qur'an elsewhere ties some of what strikes us to what our own hands have done, and some scholars say a held-back thing is worth an honest look inward before you call it luck.
On this view, maybe the paint day was rushed. Both readings are inside the tradition, and neither one turns into blame or into shrugging.

teach.h: NONE CAN GIVE WHAT YOU WITHHOLD.
teach.b: And here's a line to tell a friend tonight: right after their prayers, Muslims say the Prophet's words, O Allah, none can withhold what You give, and none can give what You withhold.
The word for withhold there shares its root with today's Name.

how: After the prayer, Muslims say the Prophet's words: O Allah, none can withhold what You give, and none can give what You withhold.

o: the Forbidder, who bans what we enjoy
the Preventer, who holds harm back
the Gatekeeper, who keeps people out

games.q: two readings of a closed door — tap the pairs.
p: the closed door as a mirror
none can give what You withhold

s: if something is withheld from you, it always means you did wrong
the Qur'an says you may hate a thing which is good for you; the door can be protection.
the Qur'an says you may love a thing which is bad for you
"it may happen that ye love a thing which is bad for you. Allah knoweth, ye know not."
the words Muslims say after prayer include: none can give what You withhold
the Prophet's words: none can withhold what You give, none can give what You withhold.

games.q: you lean toward 'every closed door is protection.' your friend says a closed door can also be a reason to look at yourself. what's the best case for your friend's side?
o: the Qur'an also ties some hardship to our own hands, so a look inward is honest.
closed doors always mean punishment, so feeling guilty is the right response.
God never closes doors at all; things just happen at random.
games.why: both readings live inside the tradition. the mirror view isn't about guilt; it asks for an honest look before calling it luck.

practice: Count back through the past year for things that didn't happen: a near miss on the road, a plan that fell through and turned out lucky, a sharp thing you almost said. Touch one finger for each.
Let every finger be a quiet thank you, to God if you pray, or simply to the moment that held back.

wordCard.voice: Al-Mani'. The Preventer, who withholds harm, and whose holding back can be part of His giving.

orig.note: Arabic: the Preventer, from the traditional list of the Names; the same root is in the post-prayer words la mani'a, none can withhold.

carryVoice: Your line: harm withheld, even on the days that only look like loss. See you tomorrow.
